prompt: A shop sells goods for 1,000 plus 10% sales tax (VAT), collected in cash. Record the sale (ignore cost of sales).

reasoning: Tax collected for the government is not revenue; the company is an agent.
It is a liability until paid over.

why_it_matters: Tax collected sits temporarily in cash: it inflates cash balances and CFO around payment dates.
common_trap: Recording 1,100 as revenue.

prompt: Gross wages are 10,000. Income tax of 1,500 and employee social-security contributions of 700 are withheld; the rest is paid in cash. Record the payroll.

reasoning: The expense is the gross wage.
Withholdings are owed to the tax authorities: a liability.

why_it_matters: Unpaid payroll taxes are a priority claim in distress; growing balances can signal cash strain.
common_trap: Expensing only the net pay.

prompt: The employer's own social-security contribution on the payroll is 900, payable next month. Record it.

reasoning: Employer contributions are an extra cost on top of gross wages.

why_it_matters: Total employment cost exceeds gross salary; use it when sizing cost-reduction programmes.
common_trap: Deducting the employer's contribution from employees' pay.

prompt: Sales of 200,000 carry a standard one-year assurance warranty. Expected warranty costs are 3% of sales. Record the provision at year end (no claims yet).

reasoning: An assurance-type warranty is a cost of the sale: provide when the sale is made (IAS 37).

why_it_matters: Falling warranty provisions as % of sales lift margins; check against actual claims history.
common_trap: Expensing warranty costs only when repairs are made.

prompt: Lawyers say the company will probably lose a lawsuit; the best estimate of the settlement is 150,000. Record the provision.

reasoning: Present obligation from a past event, probable outflow, reliable estimate: recognise a provision.
Measure at the best estimate.

why_it_matters: Provisions are judgements; releases later can boost profit. Track movements in the provisions note.
common_trap: Only disclosing because the case is not yet decided.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: IAS 37: recognise if probable (more likely than not, >50%); if a range with equal likelihood, use the midpoint.
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: ASC 450: recognise if probable (a higher threshold, 'likely to occur'); if no best estimate in a range, use the low end.

prompt: Employees have earned bonuses of 12,000 for the year under a formula in their contracts; they will be paid in March. Record the year-end accrual.

reasoning: The bonus was earned this year: accrue it.
A legal or constructive obligation exists at year end.

why_it_matters: Bonus accruals that swing with profit dampen earnings volatility; under-accrual flatters a weak year.
common_trap: Expensing bonuses when paid.

prompt: A loan is due 3 months after year end. Two weeks after year end (before the statements are issued) the company signs an agreement to refinance it for 5 years. How is the loan classified under IFRS?
options: Current, because the refinancing agreement did not exist at the reporting date
Non-current, because it was refinanced before issue
It is removed from the balance sheet

reasoning: IAS 1 looks at the right to defer settlement that exists at year end.
Post-year-end refinancing is a non-adjusting event (disclose).

why_it_matters: A large current debt figure may be about to be refinanced; read the subsequent-events note before panicking (or relaxing).
common_trap: Applying the US rule under IFRS.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: Non-current only if, at the reporting date, there is a right to defer settlement for at least 12 months.
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: ASC 470: may be non-current if refinanced (or a financing agreement is signed) before the statements are issued.

book_ref.section: Short-Term Obligations Expected to Be Refinanced

prompt: A lawsuit against the company is possible but not probable to succeed. What does IAS 37 require?
options: Disclose it as a contingent liability (unless the possibility of outflow is remote)

reasoning: Probable → provision; possible → disclosure; remote → nothing.

why_it_matters: Contingent-liability notes can contain risks larger than the company's equity.
common_trap: Provisioning for every possible claim, or disclosing nothing.

prompt: The company expects to win a lawsuit it filed, receiving 500,000, but the case is ongoing. How is it treated under IFRS?
options: Disclose as a contingent asset if an inflow is probable; recognise only when it is virtually certain

reasoning: Gains are recognised only when virtually certain.
Asymmetric with losses, which are provided when probable.

why_it_matters: Expected legal wins are upside not in the numbers; don't double count them in valuations that already assume them.
common_trap: Recognising probable gains.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: Contingent asset: disclose if probable; recognise when virtually certain.
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: Gain contingencies are not recognised until realised or realisable; disclosure must avoid misleading implications.

prompt: 1,000 products are under warranty. 10% are expected to have minor defects costing 50 each and 5% major defects costing 400 each. Warranty provision (expected value)?

reasoning: Total 25,000

why_it_matters: Provisions for large populations use expected values; single obligations use the most likely outcome.
common_trap: Using the most likely outcome (no defect) and providing nothing.

prompt: 20 employees each have 3 days of unused paid holiday that carries forward. Daily pay is 200. Accrued liability?
why_it_matters: Accumulating holiday is a real liability that grows with headcount.
common_trap: Ignoring unused holiday because no cash is due yet.

prompt: A decommissioning provision will be paid in 20 years. How is it measured under IAS 37?
options: At the present value of the expected outflow; the discount unwinds each year as a finance cost
At zero until the work starts
At the current cost of the work, undiscounted

reasoning: Provisions are discounted when the time value of money is material.
The unwinding is shown in finance costs, not operating costs.

why_it_matters: Discount-rate changes can move large provisions (oil, utilities) and equity significantly.
common_trap: Booking the unwinding in operating expenses.

prompt: The board approves a plan to close a factory next year, but nothing has been announced or started by year end. Can a restructuring provision be recognised?
options: No: a constructive obligation requires a detailed formal plan AND a valid expectation raised in those affected (announcement or start)
Yes, as soon as the board decides
Yes, for all future losses of the factory

reasoning: A board decision alone does not create an obligation; management could still reverse it.
Future operating losses are never provided for.

why_it_matters: Early restructuring provisions were once used to create reserves for later release; IAS 37 limits this.
common_trap: Providing for future operating losses of the business being closed.

prompt: Provision recognition criteria (IAS 37)

answer.meaning: Recognise a provision when there is a present obligation (legal or constructive) from a past event, an outflow is probable, and the amount can be reliably estimated.
answer.formula: Measure at the best estimate; discount if material; review each year
answer.interpretation: If not all three are met → contingent liability (disclose) or nothing (if remote).
answer.high_signals: Large or rising provisions: real risks, or reserves being built.
answer.low_signals: Releases boosting profit: check whether the original estimate was inflated.

why_it_matters: The provisions note shows additions, uses and releases: the trail of earnings management if any.
common_trap: Recognising provisions for future costs with no past event (e.g. future repairs).

prompt: Current liability

answer.meaning: A liability expected to be settled in the normal operating cycle or within 12 months, held for trading, or with no right at year end to defer settlement for 12 months.
answer.formula: Includes trade payables, accruals, current tax, current portion of long-term debt, short-term borrowings, unearned revenue

why_it_matters: Liquidity analysis compares current liabilities with cash, CFO and committed facilities.
common_trap: Forgetting the current portion of long-term debt.

prompt: Current assets 300, current liabilities 200 (ratio 1.5x). The company pays 50 of trade payables in cash. New current ratio?

reasoning: Both sides fall by 50: 250 / 150 = 1.67x
explanation.shortcut: When the ratio is above 1, paying down liabilities raises it.

why_it_matters: Year-end payments to suppliers can window-dress the current ratio.
common_trap: Thinking the ratio is unchanged because working capital is unchanged.

prompt: A retailer sells gift cards. How are unredeemed cards treated?
options: As a contract liability until redeemed; expected breakage (cards never used) is recognised as revenue in proportion to redemptions
As revenue only when they expire

reasoning: Cash received for future goods is a liability.
Under IFRS 15, expected breakage is recognised in line with the pattern of redemptions.

why_it_matters: Breakage assumptions can quietly lift revenue; check the estimate when it changes.
common_trap: Recognising revenue at the point of selling the card.

prompt: A company's profit beat expectations by 8% this year. The provisions note shows 'releases of unused provisions' equal to 7% of profit. How do you read it?

answer.model_answer: Most of the beat comes from releasing provisions, not from operations. That can be legitimate (a lawsuit settled for less than expected), but it can also be a 'cookie jar': provisions over-estimated in good years and released to meet targets. Check: which provisions were released and why; history of releases vs additions; whether the provisions were booked by previous management (big bath); timing relative to targets and bonuses; cash utilisation of provisions. For valuation, exclude the release from underlying profit and treat any pattern as a governance concern.

reasoning: Quantify the release vs the beat, then test the reason.

why_it_matters: Provision releases are one of the easiest levers to hit a number.
common_trap: Taking the beat at face value.

prompt: The board declares a cash dividend on 15 December, payable on 15 January. At 31 December the dividend is…

reasoning: Declaration creates an obligation to shareholders.
Dividends declared after year end are disclosed, not recognised (IAS 10).

why_it_matters: Declared dividends reduce net cash available; include them in near-term cash needs.
common_trap: Recognising dividends declared after year end.

prompt: A company signs a one-year note with a face value of 10,000 and no stated interest, receiving 9,400 in cash. What is the effective cost?
options: 0%, because the note has no interest rate

reasoning: The 600 discount is interest.
Effective rate = 600 / 9,400 = 6.38%.

why_it_matters: Zero-coupon or discounted borrowings still carry interest; it is just hidden in the discount.
common_trap: Thinking non-interest-bearing notes are free.
